newsitem.title: GERMANY: German recovery to stutter, then pick up - analysts.
newsitem.headline: German recovery to stutter, then pick up - analysts.

text.p: Germany's recovery may falter in the fourth quarter but will pick up in 1997, a key year when European Union members must earn their economic spurs to qualify for the planned single currency, analysts said on Wednesday.
Their prediction comes against a backdrop of strong exports, a firm dollar and low inflation and interest rates and despite the mixed picture painted by the latest economic data.

Industry orders in October, as reported on Wednesday, rose by 2.9 percent month-on-month after a sharp 3.4 percent fall in September. Industrial output data released the previous day, however, showed a fall of 1.8 percent in October after a drop of 0.6 percent.
The analysts said gross domestic product in the fourth quarter would struggle to add to the gain of close to one percent it made in the third quarter.
Although the 1.0 percent third quarter rise reported on Wednesday outstripped most forecasts, it was slower than the 1.5 percent growth in the spring period.
But with industry stocks low the orders pickup could soon feed through into output.
"It is clear that fourth quarter growth will be weaker," said economist Gerhard Grebe at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, who forecasts final quarter GDP growth of 0.3 percent.
Next year would be better, howeve. He expected the economy to chug along with growth averaging 0.5-0.6 percent per quarter and full-year 1997 growth at around 2.3 percent.

That is just below the official government forecast of 2.5 percent -- a critical figure since it underpins government spending plans intended to meet the Maastricht treaty's deficit target and qualify for European monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

"Overall...Germany is suffering from the loose money/tight fiscal stance which has been concocted by the central bank and the government in the run-up to EMU," HSBC economist Stephen King said in a note.
"The likely result is a soggy recovery with occasional significant interruptions," King added. His 1997 growth forecast is 2.4 percent after 1.3 percent this year.
Analysts said the Ifo institute's recent survey of business confidence in western Germany for October -- seen as a key leading indicator -- also pointed to rising output.
But they also cautioned that, although the German economy is picking up, it is too dependent on exports and lacks the support of internal demand to make it decisive.
The flip-side to weak consumption is that price pressures remain low in a deflationary domestic environment. That could still leave the door open to an interest rate cut.
The Bundesbank's hawkish position on inflation has eased since a sharp autumn spike in oil prices barely registered on the retail price index, Grebe said.
That, he added, has given the central bank more scope to allow the mark to fall against the dollar, which should in turn further stoke Germany's export machine.
"(Bundesbank President Hans) Tietmeyer has been saying he favoured a strong dollar," Grebe said. "Now he says he is not opposed to a stronger dollar."
Analysts also picked up on a 3.2 percent recovery in German investment in the third quarter as pointing towards broader recovery.

"We saw quite a big increase in capital spending. One thing we have been concerned about is that there hasn't been very much investment behind the recovery in the German economy," said Rob Hayward at Bank of America in London.
"Things may look a little bit better for 1997," he added.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said that a sustained recovery in both investment and output would be needed to stimulate job creation in Germany.
Seasonally adjusted unemployment hit 4.04 million in October -- the highest since unification in 1990 -- and the jobless total is expected to rise further this winter.
Analysts polled by Reuters said they expected to see a rise of between 15,000 and 45,000 in November German unemployment, which is due for release on Thursday.
